slides: Open by naming absolute geometry as the common core before choosing Euclid's parallel postulate. The lecture tracks which tools remain available: congruence transfer, triangle control, parallel pencils, products of reflections and half-turns, finite rotation groups, crystallographic restrictions, kaleidoscopes, and inversion groups.

Use the route slide to prevent the chapter from feeling like a list of isolated group facts. The story starts with congruence as the stable measuring system, then moves through parallelism, isometry products, finite rotations, lattice restrictions, spherical kaleidoscopes, and hyperbolic inversion dynamics.

The proof dependency graph is a useful map for this chapter because many later classification results rest on early congruence tools. Point out that the graph is acyclic, has fifteen nodes and thirteen edges, and explicitly connects congruence results to finite isometry classification.

Congruence is the laboratory for what absolute geometry can still measure. Segment transfer and length addition have zero error in the notebook checks, while the triangle side comparison is only at roundoff, so congruence remains a reliable invariant before any parallel axiom is chosen.

Parallelism is presented carefully because the chapter refuses to assume Euclid's fifth postulate. The shared ideal endpoint model gives zero tangent-angle discrepancy, while ultraparallel lines are inspected through a common perpendicular with a small numerical x-coordinate error.

This slide turns isometry composition into computable structure. A product of half-turns and a product of parallel reflections both match their predicted motions at roundoff, and the Donkin loop norm vanishes, so the group language is backed by explicit transformation checks.

Finite rotation groups are the bridge from elementary isometries to classification. The notebook verifies tetrahedral and octahedral rotation counts, checks signature equations for the named spherical groups, and then visualizes axes so students can see why algebraic counts are geometric.

Crystallographic restriction is where absolute geometry meets lattice symmetry. Only rotation periods one, two, three, four, and six survive in a lattice, and the chapter's table organizes thirty-two crystal classes across seven systems with four finite isometry extension patterns nearby.

The kaleidoscope slide connects finite reflection chambers with triangle signatures. The octahedral chamber has angles pi over four, pi over three, and pi over two, producing forty-eight signed permutation chambers and an area matching the sphere area divided by that chamber count.

Close with inversion-generated groups because they show the same absolute toolkit extending beyond finite spherical behavior. The signature six, three, three has reciprocal sum five sixths, the orbit has one hundred sixty-seven sampled points, and the involution and orthogonal-circle residuals remain at roundoff.
